source.title_on_document: Fostering Innovation with Generative AI: A Study on Human-AI Collaborative Ideation and User Anonymity

supplement.holds: The paper refers to no supplement or online appendix. All statistics are in the text (Section 5) and Figures 5 to 8. The system code is on GitHub.

paper_design_summary: Master's students in a course on information system design (29 who consented) used AI-deation, a group ideation app, for three 3-minute rounds. Participants were randomly divided into a human-only condition and a condition where a GPT-3.5 Turbo 'AI collaborator' added two ideas to the group's pool each round; in both conditions an LLM 'idea editor' reformulated every submitted idea for anonymity. Participants rated ideas for novelty, two authors rated ideas for innovation, and the paper also compares AI-generated ideas with participants' ideas.

studies.label: Classroom group-ideation experiment with AI-deation (human-only vs human and AI collaborator)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Condition: human-only (baseline) vs human and AI collaborator (AI collaborator suggests two new ideas per round). Both conditions used AI-deation with the LLM idea editor.
assignment.quote: In this experiment, we randomly divided the participants into two conditions. The baseline condition (human-only) involved only participants generating ideas, while the treatment condition in the treatment condition (human and AI collaborator) had the AI collaborator suggesting two new ideas at each round.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 346), end of Section 4

arms.name: Human and AI collaborator
arms.description: Group ideation in AI-deation; GPT-3.5 Turbo AI collaborator posts two new ideas into the group pool each round (48 AI ideas, 38.71% of ideas in this condition); LLM idea editor reformulates submitted ideas.

arms.name: Human-only (baseline)
arms.description: Group ideation in AI-deation without the AI collaborator; the LLM idea editor still reformulates submitted ideas.

participants.exclusions: 32 students attended the course and 29 consented to the study (p. 345). The paper does not say whether randomization took place before or after consent; 29 participants (13 control, 16 treatment) are analyzed.
participants.who: Master's students in General Management in a 6 ECTS course on information system design; 9 male, 23 female among the 32 attendees; most not native English speakers
participants.country: not_stated ("our University"; author affiliations are EPFL and University of Neuchâtel)
participants.quote: Thirty-two students (9 male, 23 female) attended the course, and 29 consented to the study.
participants.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 345), Section 4; arm counts PDF p. 5 (printed p. 346), Section 5

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-3.5 Turbo (OpenAI) for both the AI collaborator and the idea editor
ai_tool.how_used: At the end of each round the AI collaborator receives the problem and the other participants' ideas and generates one 'disruptive, out-of-the-box' idea (the evaluation section says two new ideas per round) that is added to the group pool, which participants see in the next round. In both arms an LLM idea editor reformulates each submitted idea into neutral language for anonymity (refinement).

task.description: Collaborative group ideation on a complex problem in AI-deation (example shown: 'How might we motivate people to change their behaviour to improve their health and well-being?'); participants propose ideas or build on others' ideas (max 200 characters), then rate all group ideas for novelty and usefulness on 5-point scales.
task.duration: Three rounds of three minutes each, in one class session

outcomes.name: Novelty of participants' ideas as rated by participants
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Peer ratings: participants rated every idea of their group on a 5-point Likert novelty scale. Ideas analyzed: control 77, treatment 76 participant ideas (p. 346). The paper does not say whether the test uses individual ratings or per-idea averages. Mann-Whitney U test after Shapiro-Wilk showed non-normality.

contrasts.reported: Mann-Whitney U = 3501.5, p-value = .983 (no significant difference); Shapiro-Wilk human-only W_A = .95, p = .0024; distributions in Figure 6 (boxplots, no means printed)
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 346), Section 5.2; Figure 6, PDF p. 6 (printed p. 347)

outcomes.name: Innovation of participants' ideas as rated by two authors
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The two first authors rated all ideas, blind to team, condition, and author and in randomized order, on the 5-level innovation scale of Shaer et al. (2024): 'To what extent does the idea reflect how original and creative the idea is, breaking away from the conventional or existing solutions to the problem statement?' Disagreements of 1 or more were discussed; final inter-rater correlation r(350) = .79. One-sided Mann-Whitney U test.

contrasts.reported: Mann-Whitney U = 2803, p-value = .8 (did not significantly differ); Shapiro-Wilk human-only W_A = .85, p < .001; human and AI collaborator W_B = .84, p < .001; Figure 7 boxplots
contrasts.locator: PDF pp. 6-7 (printed pp. 347-348), Section 5.2; Figure 7, PDF p. 7 (printed p. 348)

outcomes.name: Number of ideas generated per participant
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of ideas submitted by each participant (I_p). Welch's t-test after Shapiro-Wilk (W = .9, p = .2). Overall mean 5.3 ideas per participant.

contrasts.reported: Welch t(24.6) = 1.33, p-value = .2 (not significant); control 13 participants submitted 77 ideas, treatment 16 participants submitted 76 ideas; Figure 8 boxplots
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 348), Section 5.2, Figure 8; counts PDF p. 5 (printed p. 346), Section 5

outcomes.name: Novelty of AI-generated ideas vs participants' ideas (participant ratings)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Same participant novelty ratings as S1-O1. Compares the 48 ideas the AI collaborator generated with participants' ideas; the paper does not say whether participants' ideas from both conditions are pooled. One-sided Mann-Whitney U test.

contrasts.reported: Mann-Whitney U = 4463, p-value = .012 (AI ideas more novel); Shapiro-Wilk W_bot = .92, p = .004; W_participants = .97, p = .006; Figure 6
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 346), Section 5.2; Figure 6, PDF p. 6 (printed p. 347)

outcomes.name: Innovation of AI-generated ideas vs participants' ideas (author ratings)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Same author innovation ratings (Shaer et al. 2024 scale) as S1-O2. One-sided Mann-Whitney U test.

contrasts.reported: Mann-Whitney U = 1629, p-value < .001 (AI ideas more innovative); Shapiro-Wilk W_bot = .93, p = .008; W_participants = .84, p < .001; Figure 7
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 347), Section 5.2; Figure 7, PDF p. 7 (printed p. 348)

company_involvement.description: No company involvement stated. Funding: Swissuniversities P8 digital skills program and EPFL Collaborative Research on Science and Society program. The system uses the OpenAI GPT-3.5 Turbo API.

eligibility.reason: Participants were randomly divided between a human-only condition and a condition with a GPT-3.5 AI collaborator, and ideas were rated for novelty and innovation (criteria 1 and 3 met). Only 29 people were analyzed (13 control, 16 treatment; 32 attended, 29 consented), far below 50, so the study fails criterion 2. The 201 ideas do not count toward the threshold. List in the screening report as a randomized experiment with fewer than 50 participants.

one_line_finding: With 29 Master's students, adding a GPT-3.5 AI collaborator to group ideation did not change the novelty (Mann-Whitney U = 3501.5, p = .983) or rated innovation (U = 2803, p = .8) of participants' ideas or the number of ideas (Welch t(24.6) = 1.33, p = .2), although AI-generated ideas were rated more novel (U = 4463, p = .012) and more innovative (U = 1629, p < .001) than participants' ideas (pp. 346-348, Figures 6-8).
open_questions: Design class: the experiment ran in one class session of a Master's course, coded field_rct (coursework); a lab_rct coding (supervised session) is also defensible.

Comparison type: both arms used the LLM idea editor that reformulated submitted ideas, so the contrast is coded ai_design (AI collaborator plus editor vs editor only); it would be ai_vs_bau if the editor is treated as part of the platform rather than as AI assistance.

Randomization unit: the text says participants were randomly divided, but ideation happened in groups (abstract: 'groups solved complex problems'); the paper does not say whether whole groups or individuals were assigned, nor how many groups each arm had.
The paper does not say whether randomization covered the 32 attendees or the 29 who consented.
Statistical tests treat ideas (or ratings) as independent observations; no participant-level or group-clustered analysis for novelty and innovation.
notes: Self-reported outcomes not listed as output outcomes: S-UEQ usability (mean 0.2, neutral) and 13 Likert items on the idea editor and the activity (single-sample t-tests, Figure 5, p. 346), plus a thematic analysis of five open questions (Section 6). These are self_report and do not qualify under criterion 3. The paper notes no control prevented participants from using other AI systems such as ChatGPT before submitting ideas (p. 346). No means or standard deviations are printed for any outcome; distributions appear only as boxplots in Figures 6 to 8.
